323.title: Mary, mother of the Church (CCC 963–970)
323.hook: her role points always to her son
323.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Hail Mary on its own and in the rosary, and since 2018 keep the memorial of Mary, Mother of the Church, on the Monday after Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the communion of saints: the living, the dead, and the saints, one family. Your line was one family. Whose name did you say out loud? Today, the one Catholics call the mother of that family. Day three hundred twenty-three.

There's a kind of icon, very old, that you'll find in Greek, Russian and Catholic churches alike. Mary is holding the child Jesus on one arm. Her face isn't turned to you, exactly. And her other hand is open, palm up, gesturing toward the child. The icon has a Greek name, Hodegetria: she who shows the way. People sometimes imagine Catholic devotion to Mary as a spotlight on her. The oldest pictures of her have her pointing away from herself. Today, what the Church says her role is, in one gesture.
screen: `AN OLD ICON.` → `HER HAND POINTS TO THE CHILD.` → `SHE WHO SHOWS THE WAY.`

segments.voice: First, her last words in the Gospels. At a wedding in Cana, the wine runs out. Mary tells Jesus, then turns to the servants and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." That's the last thing John's Gospel records her saying. Not look at me. Do what he tells you. Second, the cross. Near the end, Jesus sees his mother and the disciple he loved standing by. "Woman, behold thy son." Then to the disciple: "Behold thy mother." And from that hour, John says, the disciple took her into his own home. Catholics read that disciple as standing for every believer: Jesus giving his mother to the whole Church. That's why Pope Paul VI, during the Second Vatican Council, formally called her Mother of the Church. Third, what the Catechism says about her role. Her place in the Church can't be separated from her union with Christ. She's the first disciple, the model of faith and love. She prays for the Church as a mother prays for her children. And the Catechism is careful: her role in no way hides or takes away from Christ as the one mediator. It shows his power. Fourth, where Christians differ. Orthodox Christians honor her deeply as Theotokos, God-bearer, and ask her prayers too. Many Protestants honor her as the mother of Jesus and a model of faith, but don't pray to her. Catholics pray the Hail Mary, which begins with the angel's greeting in Luke: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." And every line of it ends up pointing to her son.
screen: `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY, DO YE.` · `BEHOLD THY MOTHER.` · `IT SHOWS CHRIST'S POWER, NOT HERS.` · `WHERE CHRISTIANS DIFFER.` · then, large: `SHE POINTS TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one Hail Mary for the Church. Settle, and breathe. If you pray it, pray one Hail Mary slowly, for the whole Church: its people, its wounds, its saints and sinners. Let each phrase take a breath. If you don't pray it, picture the old icon instead: the mother, the child, the open hand. Follow where the hand points. Stay there until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mary. The mother of Jesus, whom Catholics call Mother of the Church: the first disciple, whose whole role, the Church says, is to point to her son. Today's word.
Your line: she points to him. Today, when someone praises you, try pointing past yourself, to the people or the grace that made it possible. Day three hundred twenty-three.

324.title: Death (CCC 1005–1014)
324.howItsDone: Catholics receive ashes on Ash Wednesday with the words remember that you are dust, pray for a holy death, and many keep November as a month of remembering the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary: the mother whose hand points to her son. Your line was she points to him. Did you point past yourself when someone praised you? Today, we begin the last things: death, judgment, and what comes after. Day three hundred twenty-four.

Ash Wednesday. A line of people shuffles toward the front of the church: office workers on a lunch break, kids in school uniforms, an old man with a cane. One by one, a priest or a minister presses a thumb of gray ash onto each forehead, in the shape of a cross, and says a sentence nobody would put on a greeting card: remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return. And here's the strange thing. People line up for it. Some years it's one of the busiest days in the church calendar. Today, why Catholics want to be reminded.
screen: `ASH WEDNESDAY.` → `YOU ARE DUST.` → `PEOPLE LINE UP FOR IT.`

segments.voice: First, the words. On Ash Wednesday the Church uses God's words to Adam, in the Douay-Rheims: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." In Latin, memento, homo, quia pulvis es: remember, human, that you are dust. That word memento, remember, gives us today's phrase: memento mori, remember that you will die. Second, what the Church says death is. The Catechism is honest: death is the end of earthly life, and it is natural, and it is also, in Christian teaching, a consequence of sin, something God did not originally want for us. But it says Christ has changed its meaning. Because he died and rose, Catholics say, death is no longer only an end. It can be a passage. Paul could write to the Philippians of "having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ." Francis of Assisi, near his own death, added a verse to his Canticle of the Creatures praising God for our Sister Death. Third, why remember it. Not to be morbid. The Catechism says remembering death reminds us that we have limited time to make something of our lives. The old litany of the saints even asks to be spared a sudden and unprepared death: not to be spared death, but to meet it ready. Fourth, what it does to a Tuesday. Think about what changes when you remember you'll die: the grudge looks smaller, the phone call to your mother looks bigger. Catholic saints kept skulls on their desks for exactly this reason. Not fear. Focus. Remember you will die, so you live like you mean it.
screen: `DUST THOU ART.` · `A PASSAGE, NOT ONLY AN END.` · `SISTER DEATH.` · `LIMITED TIME: LIVE IT.` · then, large: `MEMENTO MORI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: what you'd want said of you. Settle, and breathe. Imagine, gently, the day people gather to remember you. Not the sad part. Just the words. What would you want someone who loved you to say? Not your job title. Something like: she always had time. He made people laugh. They never gave up on anyone. Let one sentence come. Hold it. Later today, write it down. If you pray, you can ask for help to become it. The bell holds the time.
Memento mori. Latin for remember that you will die: an old Christian practice of keeping death in view, not out of fear, but to live well. Today's word.
Your line: remember you will die. Today, write down your one sentence, and do one thing that makes it a little more true. Day three hundred twenty-four.

325.title: Judgment (CCC 1021–1022)
325.hook: at death each person is judged by love
325.howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Creed that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, and many make a nightly examination of conscience, looking back over the day with the question of how they loved.

segments.voice: Yesterday, memento mori: remembering death to live well. Your line was remember you will die. Did you write down your sentence? Today, what Catholics say happens the moment after. Day three hundred twenty-five.

Hear the word judgment and most of us picture a courtroom. A huge book. Every lie you ever told, read out loud. A stern face, a gavel. Maybe a scale, with your good deeds on one side and your bad ones on the other, and you watching to see which way it tips. Now hold that picture next to a sentence written by a sixteenth-century Spanish friar you met earlier on this path, John of the Cross: at the evening of life, he said, we will be judged on love. Not on the scale. On love. Today, what the Church means.
screen: `A COURTROOM, A BOOK, A GAVEL.` → `A SCALE THAT TIPS.` → `JUDGED ON LOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. The letter to the Hebrews says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment." The Catechism teaches that each person receives this judgment at the very moment of death. It's called the particular judgment, because it's about one particular life. Second, it's immediate. The Catechism says that at death each soul, in that moment, enters either a purification, or heaven directly, or chooses to be separated from God. Catholics point to the thief crucified next to Jesus, who asked only to be remembered, and heard: "this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." Not someday. Today. Third, on love. The Catechism quotes John of the Cross's line about being judged on love at the evening of life. It fits Jesus's own story of the sheep and the goats, where the question isn't how much you knew but whether you fed the hungry. Catholics say that at death a person sees their life in Christ's light, and the question is simply how much they loved, and whether they accepted or refused his love. Fourth, two judgments. The Church also speaks of a final judgment at the end of time, when Christ returns and everything, the whole of history, is brought into the light. The particular judgment is one life. The last judgment is all of them together. And the one who judges, Catholics say, is the same one who died for the person being judged. Justice, yes. But from someone who wants you home.
screen: `ONCE TO DIE, AND AFTER, JUDGMENT.` · `THIS DAY, IN PARADISE.` · `JUDGED ON LOVE.` · `ONE LIFE, THEN ALL OF THEM.` · then, large: `JUDGED BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: examine one relationship. Settle, and breathe. Choose one person close to you: a partner, a parent, a child, a friend, a coworker. Look at the last month with them honestly, in a kind light. Where did you love well? Name it. Where did love run thin, a short word, a missed call, a silence? Name that too, without beating yourself up. Then ask one question: what would more love look like here, this week? If you pray, you can ask for help to do it. The bell holds the time.
Judgment. In Catholic teaching, the moment at death when each life is seen in Christ's light, and judged on love, followed by a final judgment at the end of time. Today's word.
Your line: judged by love. Today, do the one thing more love would look like with the person you chose. Day three hundred twenty-five.

326.title: Purgatory (CCC 1030–1032)
326.hook: a purifying for those who die in God's friendship but not yet whole
326.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead at every Mass, have Masses offered for loved ones who have died, and keep All Souls Day on November 2, when many visit cemeteries to pray.

segments.voice: Yesterday, judgment: each life seen in Christ's light, and judged on love. Your line was judged by love. What did more love look like with your person? Today, what the Church says about those who die loving God, but not yet whole. Day three hundred twenty-six.

Imagine you're invited to the most important dinner of your life. The host is someone you love. You've been working in the garden all day, and you're covered in dirt, sweaty, a scratch on your arm. You're absolutely welcome. The invitation is real and it isn't taken back. But would you want to walk in like that? Most of us would say: give me a minute. Let me wash first. That minute, the wanting to be clean before you sit down with the one you love, is close to what the Catholic Church means by one of its most misunderstood words.
screen: `INVITED TO THE DINNER.` → `COVERED IN DIRT.` → `LET ME WASH FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. The Catechism says that those who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are assured of their eternal salvation. After death they undergo a purification, so as to have the holiness needed to enter the joy of heaven. The Church calls this final purification purgatory, from the Latin purgare: to cleanse. Second, what it isn't. It isn't a second chance for someone who refused God. It isn't a smaller hell. The Catechism says it's entirely different from the punishment of the damned. Everyone in purgatory is already saved. They're on their way in. Third, where it comes from. Catholics point to Paul, who says that a person whose work burns up "shall be saved, yet so as by fire." And to the second book of Maccabees, where Judas Maccabeus has an offering made for soldiers who had died, and the text says: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." From the earliest centuries Christians prayed for their dead. Orthodox Christians still do, without defining a purgatory in the same way, and most Protestants don't hold the teaching. Fourth, the fire. The Church has often spoken of a cleansing fire. Pope Benedict XVI suggested the fire might be Christ himself: that meeting his gaze burns away what's false in us, and that the pain of it is the pain of love, and it heals. On this view purgatory isn't about being punished enough. It's about being loved until you're whole.
screen: `PURGARE: TO CLEANSE.` · `ALREADY SAVED, ON THE WAY IN.` · `A HOLY AND WHOLESOME THOUGHT.` · `THE FIRE MAY BE HIS GAZE.` · then, large: `PURIFIED BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for the dead. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has died, maybe someone you remembered a few days ago, or someone no one else remembers anymore. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, or with the old line: eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. If you don't pray, hold them in love, and wish them whole. Then widen it: all the dead who have no one to pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Purgatory. From the Latin for cleansing: the final purification, Catholics believe, of those who die in God's friendship but aren't yet whole. Today's word.
Your line: purified by love. Today, say one prayer or one good word for someone who has died, and one for someone still living who's hard to love. Day three hundred twenty-six.

327.title: Hell (CCC 1033–1037)
327.hook: the Church teaches it as self-exclusion from God, and prays that none be lost
327.howItsDone: At Mass the Church prays to be saved from final damnation, and many Catholics add the Fatima prayer to each decade of the rosary, asking that all souls be led to heaven, especially those most in need of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, purgatory: a cleansing for those already on their way into heaven. Your line was purified by love. Who did you pray for, or remember? Today, the hardest of the last things, told carefully. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

Outside the old walls of Jerusalem there's a valley. Its Hebrew name is Ge Hinnom, the valley of Hinnom. In the Bible's darkest chapters, it was a place of terrible worship, and the prophets cursed it. Later, tradition says, it became associated with burning and refuse. When Jesus warned his listeners about the ultimate loss, he used that valley's name. In Greek it became Gehenna, and English Bibles usually translate it as hell. So the word starts with a real place people could point to. Today, what the Catholic Church teaches it means, and what the Church does about it.
screen: `A VALLEY OUTSIDE JERUSALEM.` → `GE HINNOM, GEHENNA.` → `A REAL PLACE, A WARNING.`

segments.voice: First, the teaching. Jesus speaks about hell often in the Gospels, and the Church takes his warnings seriously. The Catechism defines hell as a state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God and the blessed. Not a trap God springs on people. A final, free refusal of love. Second, why it's possible at all. The Catechism says we can't be united with God unless we freely choose to love him. Love can't be forced. If a person can truly say yes, they can truly say no. The chief pain of hell, the Church says, is being separated from God, the only one in whom a human being can find the life and happiness they were made for. Third, no one is sent there by design. The Catechism states that God predestines no one to go to hell. It takes a willful turning away, persisted in to the end. And it says the Gospel's warnings are a call to responsibility and to conversion, not a threat meant to frighten. Fourth, what the Church does. The Church prays that no one should be lost, and it leans on two verses. The first letter to Timothy: God "will have all men to be saved." And Second Peter: the Lord is "not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to penance." At every Mass using the Roman Canon, the Church asks to be saved from final damnation. The Church has declared many people saints, in heaven. It has never declared any particular person to be in hell. So Catholics hold two things together: the teaching is real, and the Church prays for all.
screen: `SELF-EXCLUSION, NOT A TRAP.` · `LOVE CAN'T BE FORCED.` · `GOD PREDESTINES NO ONE TO HELL.` · `THE CHURCH PRAYS NONE BE LOST.` · then, large: `THE CHURCH PRAYS FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone far from God. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who seems lost, or hard, or turned away: someone you know, or someone in the news whose cruelty you can't understand. That's the hard part. Don't excuse what they've done. Just hold them in mind as a person God made. If you pray, you can ask God to have mercy on them, and to bring them home. If you don't, simply wish them turned toward the good. The bell holds the time.
Hell. In Catholic teaching, the state of definitive self-exclusion from God, a final refusal of love, and the reason the Church prays that no one be lost. Today's word.
Your line: the church prays for all. Today, pray for, or wish good to, one person you'd rather write off. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

328.title: Heaven (CCC 1023–1029)
328.hook: seeing God face to face, beyond what eye has seen
328.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead that they may see God's face, keep All Saints Day on November 1 for all who are in heaven, and at funerals the Church sings In Paradisum, asking that the angels lead the dead into paradise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hell: the Church's teaching of a final refusal of love, and its prayer that no one be lost. Your line was the church prays for all. Who did you refuse to write off? Today, what that prayer is hoping for. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

Think of the cartoon version of heaven. Clouds. Harps. Everyone in white robes, a bit bored, forever. It's no wonder people say heaven sounds dull. Now think of a different picture. An airport arrivals gate. Someone you love, someone you haven't seen in years, comes around the corner, and your eyes meet. For one second nothing else exists. You don't need anything. You're simply full. Catholic teaching about heaven has almost nothing to do with the clouds and everything to do with that second: a face, seen at last, and never lost again.
screen: `CLOUDS, HARPS, WHITE ROBES.` → `AN ARRIVALS GATE.` → `A FACE, SEEN AT LAST.`

segments.voice: First, the promise. Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." In his day a mirror was polished metal, and you saw only a dim, wobbly image. Now we see God that way, in hints and reflections. Then, directly. First John adds: "we shall see him as he is." Second, the name. The Church calls this seeing the beatific vision, from the Latin visio beatifica: the vision that makes you happy. The Catechism describes heaven as perfect life with the Trinity, a communion of life and love with God, Mary, the angels and all the blessed. It calls heaven the fulfillment of the deepest longings of the human heart. Augustine said it at the start of his Confessions: "our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." Heaven, for Catholics, is that rest. Third, beyond words. The Catechism admits that this mystery goes beyond any understanding or description. So Scripture uses pictures: life, light, peace, a wedding feast, the Father's house, a city. Paul quotes the prophet: "That eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him." Every image is true, and none is enough. Fourth, not boring. Seeing God, Catholics say, isn't staring at a wall forever. It's endless discovery of one who has no end, together with everyone else who loves him. Face to face with God, and so, many Catholics hope, face to face again with those they've lost.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: imagine seeing someone you love again. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've lost, to death or to distance. Picture the arrivals gate, or a kitchen door opening, or a field. Picture them coming toward you. Their face. The way they'd say your name. Let yourself feel it, even if it aches. Catholics hope for this and more: that every good meeting is a hint of seeing God. If you pray, you can thank God for that person. The bell holds the time.
Beatific vision. From the Latin for the vision that makes happy: seeing God face to face, which Catholics believe is the heart of heaven. Today's word.
Your line: face to face. Today, give someone your whole face for one conversation: put the phone away, look up, and see them. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

329.title: The resurrection of the body (CCC 988–1004)
329.hook: Catholics believe the whole person, body too, will be raised
329.howItsDone: Catholics profess the resurrection of the body in the Creed, bury their dead or reverently inter their ashes in consecrated places rather than scattering them, and honor the body in funeral rites as one day to be raised.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beatific vision: seeing God face to face. Your line was face to face. Who got your whole face? Today, the part of the Creed that says the face itself, and the body it belongs to, has a future too. Day three hundred twenty-nine.

A lot of people, if you ask them what happens after death, describe something like this: the soul floats free, like a bird out of a cage, and the body is left behind like an old coat. It's a very old idea, and it feels spiritual. But in the Apostles' Creed, just before the very last line, Christians say something much stranger and more physical. Not the survival of the soul. Something about bodies. Hands, faces, the scar on your knee. The Catholic Church says the coat isn't thrown away. Today, one of the boldest lines in the Creed.
screen: `A BIRD OUT OF A CAGE?` → `AN OLD COAT LEFT BEHIND?` → `HANDS, FACES, SCARS.`

segments.voice: First, the line. The old Prayer Book prints the Apostles' Creed's ending: "The Resurrection of the body, And the life everlasting." In Latin it's even blunter: carnis resurrectionem, the resurrection of the flesh. Second, why the body. The Catechism says a human being isn't a soul trapped in a body. We are one: body and soul together. So salvation isn't escape from the body. It's the whole person, raised. The early writer Tertullian made a Latin pun: caro salutis est cardo. The flesh is the hinge of salvation. Remember cardo, the hinge, from the four virtues? God took flesh, was raised in the flesh, and, Catholics say, will raise ours. Third, what kind of body. Not a corpse stitched back together. Paul compares it to a seed and the plant it becomes: the same life, utterly changed. In the Douay-Rheims: "It is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption." The Catechism says we'll rise with our own bodies, the ones we have now, but transformed, like Christ's risen body: real, recognizable, no longer able to die. How exactly, the Catechism says, goes beyond our imagination and understanding. When: on the last day, when Christ returns. Fourth, what it means for today. If the body has a future, it isn't disposable. Paul says "your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost." So Catholics are asked to respect their own bodies and everyone else's: the sick body, the aging body, the body in the grave. This week walked the last things: Mary, death, judgment, purgatory, hell, heaven, and now the body too.
screen: `CARNIS RESURRECTIONEM.` · `BODY AND SOUL, ONE PERSON.` · `CARO SALUTIS EST CARDO.` · `A SEED AND ITS PLANT.` · then, large: `SOWN IN CORRUPTION, RISEN IN INCORRUPTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat your body with gratitude. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet. They've carried you everywhere. Thank them. Your hands, that have held people. Your lungs, filling right now without being asked. Your heart, beating since before you were born. Notice any part that hurts, or that you've been unkind to in your head. Thank that part too. If you pray, you can thank God for the body you've been given. The bell holds the time.
The resurrection of the body. The Catholic belief that on the last day the whole person, body too, will be raised and transformed, like Christ. Today's word.
screen: `THE RESURRECTION OF THE BODY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the body too. Today, do one kind thing for your body: water, a walk, sleep, a meal eaten slowly. And one for someone else's. Day three hundred twenty-nine.
